verses.text: Now king David was old and advanced in years; and they covered him with clothes, but he couldn’t keep warm.

Therefore his servants said to him, “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king. Let her stand before the king, and cherish him; and let her lie in your bosom, that my lord the king may keep warm.”
So they sought for a beautiful young lady throughout all the borders of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.
The young lady was very beautiful; and she cherished the king, and served him; but the king didn’t know her intimately.
Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” Then he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, “Why have you done so?” and he was also a very handsome man; and he was born after Absalom.
He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah, and with Abiathar the priest; and they followed Adonijah and helped him.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belonged to David, were not with Adonijah.
Adonijah killed sheep, cattle, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En Rogel; and he called all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah, the king’s servants;
but he didn’t call Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother.
Then Nathan spoke to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, saying, “Haven’t you heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith reigns, and David our lord doesn’t know it?
Now therefore come, please let me give you counsel, that you may save your own life, and your son Solomon’s life.

Go in to king David, and tell him, ‘Didn’t you, my lord, king, swear to your servant, saying, “Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne?” Why then does Adonijah reign?’
Behold,  while you are still talking there with the king, I will also come in after you and confirm your words.”
Bathsheba went in to the king in his room. The king was very old; and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.
Bathsheba bowed, and showed respect to the king. The king said, “What would you like?”
She said to him, “My lord, you swore by Yahweh  your God  to your servant, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.’
Now, behold, Adonijah reigns; and you, my lord the king, don’t know it.
He has slain cattle and fatlings and sheep in abundance, and has called all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the captain of the army; but he hasn’t called Solomon your servant.
You, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, that you should tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.
Otherwise it will happen, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be considered criminals.”
Behold, while she was still talking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
They told the king, saying, “Behold, Nathan the prophet!” When he had come in before the king, he bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.
Nathan said, “My lord, king, have you said, ‘Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne?’

For he has gone down today, and has slain cattle, fatlings, and sheep in abundance, and has called all the king’s sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar the priest. Behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, ‘Long live king Adonijah!’
But he hasn’t called me, even me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon.
Was this thing done by my lord the king, and you haven’t shown to your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”
Then king David answered, “Call Bathsheba in to me.” She came into the king’s presence and stood before the king.
The king swore, and said, “As Yahweh lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,

most certainly as I swore to you by Yahweh, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place;’ I will most certainly do this today.”
Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the earth, and showed respect to the king, and said, “Let my lord king David live forever!”
King David said, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.” They came before the king.
The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live king Solomon!’
Then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne; for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.”
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, and said, “Amen. May Yahweh, the God of my lord the king, say so.
As Yahweh has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord king David.”
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on king David’s mule, and brought him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the Tent, and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet; and all the people said, “Long live king Solomon!”
All the people came up after him, and the people piped with pipes, and rejoiced with great joy, so that the earth shook with their sound.
Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they had finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, “Why is this noise of the city being in an uproar?”
While he yet spoke, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came; and Adonijah said, “Come in; for you are a worthy man, and bring good news.”
Jonathan answered Adonijah, “Most certainly our lord king David has made Solomon king.
The king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and they have caused him to ride on the king’s mule.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king in Gihon. They have come up from there rejoicing, so that the city rang again. This is the noise that you have heard.
Also, Solomon sits on the throne of the kingdom.

Moreover the king’s servants came to bless our lord king David, saying, ‘May your God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne;’ and the king bowed himself on the bed.
Also thus said the king, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who has given one to sit on my throne today, my eyes even seeing it.’”
All the guests of Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and each man went his way.
Adonijah was afraid because of Solomon; and he arose, and went, and hung onto the horns of the altar.

Solomon was told, “Behold, Adonijah fears king Solomon; for, behold, he is hanging onto the horns of the altar, saying, ‘Let king Solomon swear to me first that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of his shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.”
So king Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed down to king Solomon; and Solomon said to him, “Go to your house.”

footnotes.content: Old age comes for us all, and with it a cold that no blanket can fix. David's days of conquest are behind him now, his vigor spent. Yet the Lord still holds His king in the palm of His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The advisors reach for the simplest remedy—a young woman's warmth. How often do we seek comfort in gentle, earthly things when our real need is deeper still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abishag of Shunem was chosen from across all Israel—the search itself speaks to David's honor, even in weakness. The Lord's servant, though diminished, was still honored by his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is a dignity in this care: Abishag served a frail man without taking from him what the covenant had held sacred. Even in our weakness, the Lord preserves what is His.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah sees an old man and sees an opening. Ambition whispers its old song: *I will be king.* But the throne is not ours to seize—it is the Lord's gift to give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A handsome son who was never told 'no'—this too is a kind of poverty. Without the shaping grace of a father's boundary, a child grows bent toward his own will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab and Abiathar circle the young prince. Power recognizes power, and the ambitious find ready allies. One man's ambition becomes two men's rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the mighty man—these stood apart, true to their oath and their God. Loyalty is its own kind of strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah throws a feast by the stone of Zoheleth, near En Rogel, gathering the king's sons and the men of Judah. The theater of rebellion: good food, many witnesses, a crown already worn in the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Solomon is not called. Neither the prophet Nathan, nor Benaiah the faithful, nor the mighty men of David. The omission itself speaks—Adonijah's rebellion excludes all who might stand in his way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan sees what is hidden and acts. The prophet carries a burden the priest does not: he must speak truth even when it unsettles the powerful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan comes to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, with counsel born of urgency: save your life and your son's. The stakes are clear and high.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan reminds Bathsheba of David's oath: Solomon *shall* reign. An oath made, a promise sworn to the Lord. Now it must be remembered and claimed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan's plan: Bathsheba will speak first, then he will come and confirm. Two witnesses to a truth that must be declared. There is wisdom in speaking together when silence means death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bathsheba enters the chamber where David lies, and Abishag is still there, serving. Even in age, even amid the whispering of the court, David remains the king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bathsheba bows low, showing the respect due a king. Courtesy is not weakness; it is the language of a heart that knows how to approach power with honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She speaks his oath back to him: Solomon *shall* reign, and sit on the throne. Words from a woman who remembered this promise when the king himself may have forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But now Adonijah reigns, she says, and the king does not know. A careful, respectful telling of what has been hidden. The king has been kept in the dark by his own court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah has slain cattle and sheep in abundance, and called the king's sons and the priests and Joab. But Solomon—the one promised—is not there. The feast itself is an act of rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel looks to you, she says. The king's word shapes the kingdom. His choice is no small thing—it is a word spoken into the future of an entire people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you sleep with your fathers, she warns, Solomon and I will be counted as criminals. Death brings its own clarity: what the king decrees today will define her tomorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Bathsheba speaks, Nathan appears at the door. God's timing is woven into human timing—the prophet arrives just as the word is being spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They announce Nathan's arrival. He enters, bows before the king—respect for the throne even as he carries a word that challenges the court's silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan asks directly: Did you say Adonijah will reign? The prophet speaks truth as a question, drawing out the king's own memory of what he has sworn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He describes the rebellion plainly: the feast, the slaughter, the shout—*Long live king Adonijah!* The feast is not a celebration; it is a coup dressed as a party.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But I am not called, Nathan says. Neither the faithful priests nor Benaiah nor Solomon. By their absence, the rebellious son reveals his fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan's question is terrible and beautiful: Did you do this without telling your servants who will sit on your throne? He names the silence as a sin of omission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's answer is swift: Call Bathsheba. The king wakes, it seems, and reclaims his throne by reclaiming his will. She enters and stands before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David swears by the living God who has redeemed his soul from all adversity. He speaks from the depth of a life lived and a God honored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king repeats his oath: Solomon shall reign and sit on my throne *in my place*. Not after, but *now*—David declares the succession in his lifetime.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bathsheba bows and speaks a blessing: *Let my lord king David live forever!* She honors him with words, though both know the years are short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Call to me Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah—the three who stood apart. David chooses the faithful to carry out his will, the ones who never wavered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take Solomon on my own mule and bring him down to Gihon. The king gives his son his own beast, his own authority made visible. It is an act of investiture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Anoint him king there at Gihon—the spring of Jerusalem, a place of water and life. Blow the trumpet, cry out: *Long live king Solomon!* Let the people hear and know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shall sit on my throne, and reign in my place, David declares. This is not a distant inheritance but an immediate claim, a kingdom received while the father still breathes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah's answer is swift: *Amen.* The mighty man blesses the king's word, joining his strength to the throne's will. Loyalty spoken aloud is its own kind of power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: May the God of David be with Solomon, Benaiah prays, and make his throne greater than yours. He asks not for the son to replace the father, but to build on what the father has left.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Cherethites and Pelethites—David's own guard—go down with Solomon to Gihon. The king's loyal men now serve the king's son. Continuity is secured by loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok takes the horn of oil from the Tent and anoints Solomon. Oil upon oil—the sign of God's choosing, visible and real. The trumpet sounds. *Long live king Solomon!* the people shout.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people come up after him, playing pipes, rejoicing with great joy. The earth shakes with their sound. Joy is the earth's response to a true king rightly chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Adonijah's feast, the sound of the trumpet reaches their ears. They know, in that moment, what the noise means: the kingdom has slipped from his grasp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan the priest's son arrives. Adonijah, with a dying hope, calls him in—surely he brings good news. But hope built on ambition is a hollow thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan speaks plainly: Our lord king David has made Solomon king. The word is already done, the oath already fulfilled. What seemed near is suddenly distant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the king's guard rode with him, Jonathan says. The authorities of the kingdom itself have moved to Solomon's side. Rebellion, seen so plainly, becomes futile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok and Nathan have anointed him king in Gihon, Jonathan reports. They have come up rejoicing; the city rings with the sound. The deed is done and declared and celebrated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon now sits on the throne of the kingdom. The fact is simple and total. Not shall be, but *is*. Anointing has made it real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's servants come to bless David, saying: May God make Solomon's name better than yours, and his throne greater. Even as David releases the crown, he receives the blessing of his servants' respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David bows on his bed and gives thanks: *Blessed be the God of Israel, who has given me one to sit on my throne, my eyes even seeing it.* He sees the future secured and gives glory to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah's guests, seized by fear, scatter and each goes his own way. The feast that promised a kingdom becomes an image of the kingdom broken. Ambition finds few willing to fall with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah flees to the altar and grasps its horns—a gesture of asylum in Israel's law. Even a rebellious son knows where mercy might be found, though he struck at the throne itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Word reaches Solomon: your brother hangs on the altar horns, begging for his life. The rebel has become a suppliant. Everything turns on how the new king will answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's answer: *If he shows himself worthy, he lives; if wickedness is found in him, he dies.* The young king speaks not from vengeance but from justice—a hard mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon sends men to bring Adonijah down; his brother bows to the new king. Readers today hear an echo: how often the Lord brings us low precisely so we might bow to His rule and find our life in submission, not in the throne we thought we deserved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
